Specifically, WASP achieves this by training a shared hypernetwork that maintains a compact user representation and outputs adapter weights in a single forward pass. As new interactions arrive, WASP updates this representation without reprocessing full interaction history, enabling continual adaptation with per-update costs independent of history length. Experiments on personalization benchmarks and chronological interaction streams show that WASP sustains high-quality personalization over long horizons under fixed compute and storage budgets. Together, these results support efficient streaming personalization and facilitate privacy-preserving on-device deployment.

Post-Training Agents for Long-Document Reasoning. Professional documents are a long-context workload that retrieval-style benchmarks do not capture. In a ten-domain enterprise collection, a task's evidence is spread across a source document of median length 27 pages (mean 48.8, maximum 873); a third of tasks rest mainly on charts, drawings, and maps; and 70.9% require two or more reasoning hops. We post-train Kimi-K2.7, an open-weight foundation model, at its full context window on 1,465 expert-authored tasks with atomic rubrics from that collection, training rank-32 adapters with one round of privileged-context on-policy self-distillation followed by two rounds of rubric-reward reinforcement learning. We render each PDF as text for training and as extracted text plus selected page images at evaluation. The smoothed RL training reward rises from 0.37 in the first tenth of the run to 0.67 in the last. On the 100-task GDP.pdf holdout, served in a 262,144-token window, strict pass (all rubric criteria met) more than doubles after the second round, from 11.0% to 24.5%, with gains across input lengths up to 240K tokens. Mean tokens generated stay flat (9,803 to 9,733), so the gain does not come from longer outputs. GPT-5.6 Sol's leaderboard strict pass is 30.7% at a measured 3,422 tokens. On 220 out-of-domain GDPval tasks, where the model runs as a long-horizon tool-using agent, mean rubric reward rises from 0.571 to 0.746 after the third round and zero-credit tasks fall from 54 to 10, while messages per task fall 18%, from 70.9 to 58.2. In paired trajectories, the third round replaces a context-thrashing retry loop with one up-front check of all sources, and verification extends from checking that files exist to checking what they contain. We argue that long-context evaluation of agents should report accuracy jointly with tokens and turns, and that datasets of long documents should ship text and image renderings alongside each PDF.

Context-Grounded Skill Internalization for Vision-Language Agents. Skill internalization offers a way for agents to learn useful behaviors from skills and use them without explicit guidance in context at inference time. A common approach is to generate demonstration trajectories with the skill in context and then fine-tune the same model on its own trajectories with the skill removed. However, this leads to the problem that the model may learn to reference the removed skill, which we named as context misalignment (CoMi). In this work, we first analyze agent behaviors related to CoMi under this common pipeline. Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and ARC-AGI-1, skill-removed fine-tuning consistently results in CoMi: 12.2-46.0% of test trajectories reference the removed skill. To address this problem, we develop Context-Grounded Skill Internalization (CGSI). CGSI uses a sentence detector to identify unsupported references and then masks or rewrites the selected sentences before fine-tuning. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of CGSI and reveal two key findings. (i) Compared with directly fine-tuning with the skill removed, CGSI reduces CoMi at test time by 72.5-94.6% while preserving task success. (ii) Compared with existing reinforcement learning-based skill-internalization baselines, CGSI achieves comparable performance with substantially less training time. CGSI also significantly reduces processing costs compared with large-scale trajectory auditing and correction.

RoboLiveMem: Is Robot Memory Solved When the World Does Not Wait?. Robot agents built on frontier vision-language models now solve most robot memory benchmarks. Does this mean they can remember what they need in a home, where people and machines keep moving things? Existing memory benchmarks cannot answer this question, because they pause the simulator while the model thinks: nothing can change during a decision, so whatever the robot remembers is still true when it acts. We introduce RoboLiveMem, a benchmark that runs the same memory tasks twice, once with the world paused while the model thinks and once with the world running. It contains 29 task families in three tiers, from 16 realistic BEHAVIOR-1K scenes of homes, workshops and a restaurant to controlled ManiSkill tasks. Every task mixes real changes with harmless look-alikes and runs without any change, so that no fixed strategy succeeds, and most tasks have a twin that keeps the change in view, which separates forgetting from acting too late. Testing 16 models on 34,176 episodes, we find three surprises. (1) Paused results hide the problem: when a remembered object changes in a realistic scene, the 8 Claude and GPT models succeed in 97% of episodes on average with the world paused, but in only 50% with the world running, and their ranking changes: Claude Opus 5.5, which never fails when paused, succeeds in 44%. (2) Speed is not the fix: slower models do no worse, and models given only 2 s per decision still fall at least 36 points below their paused success. (3) Models see the change but act on camera frames from before it ended. Looking again just before acting closes most of the realistic gap, yet when identical objects are swapped several times, all nine models we test still lose points to memory.

OWE-Bench: A long-horizon benchmark for measuring real-world engineering. We present OWE-Bench (OpenWorldEngineer-Bench), a benchmark of 26 long-horizon engineering tasks written by domain experts in software engineering, physical engineering, machine learning, and scientific computing. Tasks range from optimizing kernels and designing an aircraft, to identifying the faults responsible for an earthquake. Each task requires significant domain knowledge and engineering work, with models averaging hundreds of millions of tokens per task. Solutions are scored on practical measures such as speed, cost and accuracy, both on provided cases the agent could test against and on hidden cases that an engineer would expect from the task description. The best-performing frontier model so far, Claude Fable 5.2, scores 54.6% and averages 211 million tokens per task. We highlight two findings. First, when models are given more time, they use more test-time compute and achieve higher scores. Models also scale differently with test-time compute: GPT-6 Astra achieves higher scores at shorter time limits and at equal token use, while Claude Fable 5.2 uses more tokens at longer limits to achieve the highest overall score. Second, each model scores lower on hidden cases than on the provided cases, by an average of 18 points, which we call the deployment gap. Models also fail to predict the deployment gap, overestimating their performance on hidden test cases by an average of 21 points. We hope that OWE-Bench grounds progress toward agents whose engineering solutions perform as well in deployment as they do in testing.

Conartist: Adaptive Agentic Red-Teaming of Computer-Using Agents against Multi-Step Prompt Injection. Harnesses secure Computer-Using Agents by enforcing security constraints and defending against prompt injection attacks. However, we find that two core security mechanisms of agent harnesses remain vulnerable. First, consistency checking prevents agents from deviating from legitimate user objectives, while attackers can bypass it by embedding malicious actions that appear logically consistent with legitimate task execution. Second, risk auditing proactively examines high-risk operations. Yet, the auditing process itself would introduce additional exploitable actions that violate security boundaries. To evaluate above defects we found, we propose Conartist, a cascaded adaptive prompt injection framework comprising two progressive stages. First, Conartist employs a goal-pollution strategy to establish deceptive causal dependencies between legitimate user objectives and malicious operations, progressively embedding attack steps into legitimate task workflows. However, these task-coupled attacks remain susceptible to risk auditing. To address this limitation, Conartist further analyzes security-auditing feedback from controlled attack exploration to identify exploitable auditing patterns. Conartist then adaptively refines its deception strategies to either avoid triggering risk auditing or induce additional high-risk operations. Extensive experiments across five backbone models demonstrate the effectiveness of Conartist, achieving attack success rates of 32.12% on 576-instance tool use benchmark and 66.67% in the Reddit GUI benchmark, outperforming the SOTA attack by 14.41 and 29.17, respectively. By analyzing one of the most popular Agent, Openclaw, we furthermore concluded seven realistic exploitable attack patterns, which reveals that security mechanisms designed to prevent malicious actions can themselves be manipulated to facilitate attacks.

CARE-3D: Reinforcement Learning for Evidence Grounded Agentic Reasoning in Situated 3D Scenes. Situated 3D reasoning requires embodied agents to interpret objects, scene geometry, and viewpoint dependent spatial relations. Existing methods learn grounded interactions from supervised traces, but largely imitate prescribed evidence acquisition patterns rather than optimizing the support that the returned evidence provides for the correct answer. Moreover, outcome rewards provide limited credit for intermediate tool choices and may leave infrequent tools underexplored. An effective agent should instead adaptively decide what to ground, which tool to invoke, and how to assess the utility of returned evidence. To this end, this paper presents CARE-3D, a reinforcement post-training framework for adaptive grounded reasoning. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on grounding instructions first establishes valid interactions, after which Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) optimizes the agent while keeping the 3D grounding module frozen. CARE-3D combines Counterfactual Attribution of Returned Evidence for evidence sensitive credit assignment, and Group Coverage Sampling to preserve tool coverage. Experiments on MSQA and Beacon3D show consistent gains over SFT and GRPO using only answer and format rewards, especially in spatial reasoning and grounding answer coherence. Our code is available at \href{https://github.com/xiaoqian-UQ/CARE-3D}{CARE-3D}.

LLM-Assisted Software Migration: from Module-Level Transformation to Repository-Level Integration. Software migration adapts an existing implementation to a new language, version, API, framework, or platform while preserving its behavior. Large language models (LLMs) succeed on individual functions and modules, but this success does not readily carry over to entire repositories, particularly deployable applications. This survey reviews LLM-assisted migration from module-level transformation to repository-level integration, culminating in the delivery of complete applications. We analyze 96 sources---including 46 direct migration papers---across four perspectives: (1) supported software engineering activities, (2) model roles as editors or orchestrators, (3) orchestration workflows (agentless, single-agent, or multi-agent), and (4) enabling techniques including knowledge engineering, project context, environment feedback, and model adaptation. We then compare evaluation practices and benchmarks. Although 30 of the 46 studies target repositories, most acceptance evidence relies merely on build success, supplied tests, or static and model-based proxies. Moreover, compilation, visual similarity, test outcomes, and runtime behavior capture fundamentally distinct properties and cannot be conflated into a single success rate. We also identify critical gaps in requirements engineering support and in controlled comparisons of agent architectures. Finally, we discuss six open problems: application integration, platform differences, non-functional properties, generalization, attribution of gains, as well as cost and maintenance.

Landscape and Taxonomy of Prompt Engineering Patterns in Software Engineering. Advancements in large language models (LLMs) have enhanced their ability to handle ambiguous user instructions. However, effective prompt patterns remain crucial for usability and comprehension. This article presents a taxonomy of prompt engineering patterns for software engineering. It is based on a systematic literature review that was conducted in early 2023, when LLMs still faced significant limitations in context length and inference capabilities. Our study explores techniques that enhance the usability and reliability of LLMs, emphasizing the ongoing importance of well-designed prompts in optimizing task performance. Our findings highlight the critical role of prompt patterns in maximizing LLM's potential, even as their capabilities continue to evolve.

Memphis: A Case Study in Seeding an Agent Task from a Model's Real-World Attempt. Agent benchmarks are usually made harder by scaling up the data their tasks are built from, yet models that do well on them still fail at real work. We propose building simulated tasks from a model's own attempt at an open-ended task in the real world, so that the model's failures in the simulation resemble its failures in reality. As a case study, we had GPT-6.1 Sol manage two human workers in Cairo over chat for five shifts, with a budget of 7,000 Egyptian pounds, to build as many USB desk lamps as it could. It built two. From the real-world attempt's transcript, we build Memphis, an evaluation in a model-simulated world. Memphis is hard: GPT-6.1 Sol delivers 1.0 lamp per trial on average and repeats its real-world mistakes, buying too few stands and giving up the search for them. With a one-page hint on where to buy parts and who can wire them, it delivers 9.2. Claude Opus 5.5 delivers 2.2 without the hint and 4.6 with it. We release the task, the trials, the audits, and a redacted record of the real-world evaluation.

Can Vibe Coding Produce Accessible Websites: An Empirical Study on LLM Coding Agents and Skills. Large language model (LLM) coding agents increasingly allow developers and non-professionals to create websites through natural-language instructions, with limited inspection of the generated source code. Although this ``vibe coding'' workflow lowers barriers to software creation, it may also propagate accessibility defects at scale. We investigate the accessibility of websites generated end-to-end by contemporary coding agents and whether agent-level accessibility interventions improve their output. We generated 90 websites for three projects using combinations of three coding agents, four language models, and multiple reasoning-effort levels. We evaluated complete interaction journeys using axe-core, IBM Equal Access Accessibility Checker, and QualWeb, and converged reports to observe violation prevalence and violated WCAG Success Criterion (SC). None of the 90 baseline websites was fully accessible, with an average of 80.43 violated interface elements. 13 WCAG SCs were violated at least once across the runs. Color contrast was the most prevalent issue, followed by labeling, semantic-structure, keyboard, and visualization failures. We reran 24 matched configurations with a general accessibility Skill and a contrast-specific Skill. Both significantly improved accessibility scores, but neither eliminated violations. User testing with blind individuals corroborated the experiential effects of the detected inaccessibilities. Moreover, functional correctness decreased with the inclusion of Skills. Our findings show that accessibility does not reliably emerge from vibe coding, and agentic interventions can both improve some accessibility issues and introduce new functional ones.

Blind to What They Can Fix: A Detection Gap in Self-Improving Agents. AI agents can write programs that carry out a task without calling a model at every step, so the task runs fast and its logic stays open to inspection. Agents improve these programs by running them, studying their failures, and revising the code, a form of recursive self-improvement (RSI). We ask whether this process also yields runtime checks that can be trusted. In five task domains, with up to seven author models, agents bring their programs to high scores. Yet when the environment changes, the checks they were told to write stay silent on half or more of the resulting failures in four domains. These failures can be detected and repaired: a monitor built from records of normal runs catches most of them in three domains, and the same agents usually repair them once called. The checks do not examine the recorded relations that reveal the failures, and the strongest agent writes checks that catch most of them once told that its checks are the only thing that calls it back. An unreported failure stays unrepaired, which limits what self-improvement is worth in autonomous operation. Evaluations of self-improvement should measure not only scores but also whether a system notices its own failures.

Admitted Is Not Effective: Lessons from a Notary-Gated Retrospective Loop in an Agentic Pipeline. Agentic software development pipelines with frozen prompts can repeat the same mistakes across pull requests (PRs), yet ungoverned additions to instruction files grow without bound and do not generally improve task success. We present a retrospective loop for a four-stage large language model (LLM) pipeline in which a Retrospective agent proposes edits to learned rules every ten PRs and a Notary admits, merges, or rejects them while recording each decision in a provenance ledger. In a pre-registered study of 880 PRs on two Python repositories, the loop ran end to end and the Notary admitted 55 of 89 proposals, rejecting 8 that cited nonexistent evidence. However, held-out review comments and hidden-test resolution did not improve after ten retrospectives. Tracing each step of the loop, we found that sparse review signal (0.45 comments/PR) left little to learn from and that rules admitted on their stated evidence did not show measurable held-out effects. We derive six lessons and argue that governed loops should admit and retire every learned rule as a testable hypothesis.

Fin-RSI: A Unified Library of Financial Skills, Checks, and Self-Improvement for LLM Agents. As large language models (LLMs) become more capable, financial agents need tools they can readily discover and use. Yet financial software is fragmented across libraries with different interfaces and conventions, making it difficult to build reliable agent workflows. We present Fin-RSI, a unified Python library of financial skills, checks, and self-improvement designed for LLM agents. It brings together tools for market analysis, forecasting, portfolio construction, and trading research through shared interfaces across models and agent frameworks. Agents can find suitable tools from natural-language requests, reuse tested implementations, and improve generated programs through checking and feedback. Developers can extend the library with new tools without rebuilding integrations for each model. Across 20 open-weight models on six trading-position tasks, tool discovery increased the proportion of episodes producing valid programs from 9.7% to 29.2%; for models with at least 14 billion parameters, it rose from 23.6% to 64.6%. We release the library and benchmark as a shared resource for the community and plan to expand its tools and task coverage as financial agents evolve.

Wactorz: Self-Writing LLM Agents That Discover, Repair, and Migrate at the Edge. Most LLM agent frameworks build a crew that runs a task and exits. Physical environments (e.g., homes, labs, factory floors) need agents that stay up for months, survive their own bugs, and run on whatever hardware is already next to the sensors. We present Wactorz, an open-source runtime in which LLM-generated agents are long-lived, supervised actors: a planner turns a chat request into Python, compiles it into a new actor at runtime, and a supervisor restarts that actor alone, with its state intact, when it crashes. All coordination rides on MQTT, so agents can be spawned on, and live-migrated between, edge nodes such as a Raspberry Pi, and every internal event is a topic external systems can subscribe to. The recorded demo builds a camera-to-lamp automation from one chat request, adds a second agent that is auto-wired to the first by topic and carries a deliberate division-by-zero, watches that agent repair its own code without losing its count, then deploys a fresh Raspberry Pi node and live-migrates the agent onto it, in under four minutes of wall-clock time and \$0.13 of model usage. This extended version adds what the two-page demonstration paper could not: the Wiring view of the topic graph, Wactorz as a library for hand-written agents, how trained models are stored, sent to nodes and replaced, the security model, and the system's limitations.

Weight Coding: Evolving Web-Scale Recommenders through Direct Weight Edits with LLM Agents. Web-scale recommender models evolve primarily through retraining or fine-tuning. We propose \emph{weight coding}, a methodology for model evolution through direct, executable weight edits. A large language model (LLM) agent inspects model structure and parameters, formulates hypotheses, and implements edits using evaluation feedback. The loop progresses from localized changes to targeted searches and composition, allowing edited components to adapt to one another. A cached engine enables rapid forward evaluation without backpropagation. On Pinterest's 147M-parameter Image Search two-tower retriever, weight coding improves held-out recall@10 of production model by up to 15.0 percentage points (+24\% relative) with few edits in about 1/4 GPU hours of a full post-training finetune, while a common launch only improves around 1\%. After reinitializing the entire 13.6M-parameter interaction module randomly while retaining the surrounding trained model, searching 2,448 mixing and normalization parameters yields 9.8 points above production. Offline gains span the full funnel including dense retrieval, generative retrieval and ranking, with up to 1.37B learnable parameters and different edits for each architecture. Steering edits provide explicit control of model performance over segments like freshness and product. Weight coding requires no serving change and online A/B tests increase saves per user from the edited retrieval source by 8.4\% to 10.7\%, aligned with the target business objectives. Our results establish weight coding as a practical and useful tool for model development and and behavioral control in a real web-scale production system, with potential to extend to both pre-training and post-training stages across the funnel.

KernelShift: Benchmarking Kernel Optimization Across Evolving Hardware. Efficient AI computation depends on hardware that evolves over time, shifting the strategies needed to implement performant code. For CPU kernels, a key evolving factor is the set of available architectural extensions, which expose specialized hardware instructions that change the techniques used to optimize kernels. We study how effectively coding agents use these new, potentially unfamiliar extensions to write fast code. We introduce KernelShift, a benchmarking pipeline and a set of environments for evaluating coding agents in kernel optimization across evolving CPU architectures. Its agent-assisted, human-verified pipeline turns code repositories into benchmark instances, and its environments let agents optimize code with feedback from the target hardware. Using this pipeline, we construct 99 kernels from real-world, actively developed repositories (ncnn, llama.cpp, Arm SIMD Loops, and KleidiAI), including inference workloads derived from real model executions. KernelShift supports incorporating new kernels and hardware configurations as libraries and processors evolve. We evaluate agents with proprietary and open-weight models across progressively newer architectural extensions (Arm Neon, SVE, SVE2, and SME2), examining how performance changes as hardware evolves. On established extensions, agents beat the auto-vectorized compiler everywhere (2.4-19.8x) and exceed general-purpose libraries such as ncnn (getting up to 2.74x over its Neon kernels), but fall behind Arm's hand-tuned KleidiAI kernels (0.70x). In end-to-end inference of two LLMs, agent-written kernels achieve a 1.3-1.6x prefill speedup over llama.cpp's fast path. However, current agents do not yet reliably adapt to new extensions that require unfamiliar programming models, such as SME2's matrix tiles.

How Multi-Timescale Memory Cools Optimization: Theory and Evidence from AdEMAMix. Augmenting AdamW with multiple momentum timescales improves large language model pretraining, yet the mechanism driving these gains remains poorly understood. We identify an interaction between multi-timescale optimizer memory and the geometry of normalized networks: memory changes parameter norms and thereby controls how fast parameters rotate. Starting from exact norm dynamics under decoupled weight decay, we show that the parameter norm depends on the temporal correlation of the updates, with weight decay controlling how long these correlations influence optimization. We show how an independently weighted slow momentum can substantially increase the norm of parameters, while contributing negligible power to the instantaneous update, therefore acting as an endogenous annealing schedule. We study this mechanism in AdEMAMix for language-model pretraining. Controlled interventions show that this scheduling mechanism has clear practical consequences and is an important factor behind AdEMAMix's advantage over AdamW.

Layer-Level Control of Language Model Execution in Agent Frameworks. Agent frameworks typically orchestrate language models through prompt-and-response interfaces. We propose a harness design that exposes intermediate model states and layer-level execution controls to the agent runtime. By connecting state collection, policy fitting, and execution, the design enables policies to allocate computation within and across models based on intermediate states. We demonstrate the approach with a prototype that learns stitching bridges and state-conditioned execution policies from paired model states, then applies them during inference to select among continue, exit, and stitch. For dispatcher supervision, we select the least-computation action whose full-vocabulary next-token prediction matches the source model's full-depth prediction, using continue when neither early action matches. We train these components on a frozen proxy corpus of 5,000 typed-decision items authored using source texts sampled from WildChat conversations, then evaluate the prototype on JevBench measuring task accuracy, agreement with full-model predictions, and end-to-end latency including runtime overhead. Preliminary results show an approximately 15% reduction in mean latency while maintaining task accuracy comparable to full-model inference.

Beyond Accuracy: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Hypothesis-Driven Experiment Planning in LLM Agents. Evaluating large language model (LLM) agents on scientific tasks typically reduces to final-task accuracy, which obscures where reasoning succeeds or breaks down. We introduce a benchmark and diagnostic evaluation framework for hypothesis-driven adaptive experimental planning in closed-world system identification, instantiated in kinetic mechanism identification. The framework goes beyond final accuracy in two ways. First, we evaluate exploration behavior by quantifying the extent to which agents exhibit space-filling or corner-seeking patterns in the experimental design space. Second, we decompose the reasoning process into four interpretable steps: belief update, hypothesis discrimination, discriminative experiment design, and predictive reasoning under interventions, each scored separately on reasoning traces. Across ten LLM agents, we find that stronger agents outperform both adaptive (Bayesian optimization) and non-adaptive (Latin hypercube) baselines and exhibit exploration patterns inconsistent with naive heuristics. Decomposing reasoning reveals that the stronger agents score consistently well across all four steps, whereas weaker agents often succeed at belief update and hypothesis discrimination but are less reliable at translating them into actionable designs and sharp contrastive predictions. Independent expert annotations support predictive reasoning under our stated validation criteria, while evidence for discriminative experiment design is positive but less consistent. The results suggest a gap between recognizing plausible hypotheses and translating them into contrastive predictions, with more tentative evidence for a corresponding experiment-design bottleneck. The benchmark website is available at https://schwallergroup.github.io/beyond-accuracy/.

MobileNeTTT: a Lightweight DNN-based Time-To-Transit Estimator for Visual Navigation. Time-to-Transit (TTT) is a perceptual cue, proxy for depth, that can be computed in the visual cortex, allowing animals to estimate the time remaining to move past features in the environment. We show how TTT can be estimated and used for bio-inspired navigation of a mobile robot equipped with a monocular camera. The paper describes a lightweight neural network estimation method, named MobileNeTTT, that (1) uses the full field of view and provides a rich array of visual feature TTT estimates; (2) is relatively insensitive to camera rotation; and (3) automatically adjusts to the geometry of the path and the presence of obstacles. Because TTT is a coarse visual cue, it is far simpler to use for robot navigation than current large visual depth foundation models. Our navigation model uses a 1.95M-parameter network that is two to three orders of magnitude smaller than well-known large vision foundation models, making it able to run in real time on edge hardware. Simulation and actual laboratory experiments validate the proposed approach in dynamic and spatially complex environments. Code, data, and video are available.

Agentic Discovery of Simple Symbolic Inventory Policies. Designing simple inventory policies becomes increasingly difficult as operational features and system configurations expand. We develop an Agentic Inventory-Policy Discovery System based on explicitly defined simple operational formula (SOF) policy and template classes. Large language models (LLMs) revise symbolic structures, while a numerical engine fits parameters separately for each instance and evaluates the induced policies. Multicriteria parent selection, state-specific operational diagnostics, and reusable symbolic motifs guide structural evolution. A three-stage progression develops shared templates across instances and configurations with varying state dimensions. Experiments on 15,600 instances spanning 50 demand distributions cover lead times, perishability, their combination, and lead times with limited customer patience. The discovered templates improve aggregate empirical performance over evaluated SOF benchmarks and are competitive with policies requiring more elaborate online computations. For a lost-sales system with a three-period lead time, we develop an average-cost decomposition and prove that, under specified demand and cost conditions, a capped dual-shortfall specialization of a discovered policy strictly outperforms every policy in the considered capped base-stock benchmark class. This analysis links the performance advantage to the discovered replenishment mechanism. Together, these results highlight the potential of agentic discovery to generate simple inventory policies with strong empirical performance and identify operational mechanisms amenable to rigorous theoretical analysis.

Emotion-Aware and Context-Grounded Dialogue Agents for Personalized Video Game Interactions. We present ChatNPC, a game companion that dynamically personalizes its responses in real time based on players' emotional shifts to enhance user immersion. The model integrates sequential data, leveraging the dynamic nature of streams to benefit from player information, spoken lines, and in-game context. We leverage recent progress in LLMs' tool-calling capabilities to extract vital information from memory and recognize potential constraints for accurate reasoning, thereby tackling the complexity of NPC conversation scenarios. The task is divided into a game sentinel-guided agent (SeGent), a memory capability, and a chat planning tool for reasoning instantiation. The approach uses a lightweight game template as an information framework, with relevant details and a thorough reasoning layout. We conduct extensive experiments on a newly developed game dataset for in-game context NPC dialogue and demonstrate that ChatNPC sequentially captures players' emotional shifts over time; responses are more naturalistic and human-like with appropriate conversational cues, pauses, and sighs; and utterances remain faithful to the dynamics of in-game context and player actions, supporting narrative continuity.

EMIP: Embodied Multi-Party Interaction Platform. Experimental platforms that enable multiple participants to engage in spoken dialogue and perform physical actions concurrently in a shared environment are important for studying cooperation between humans and embodied AI agents. In this paper, we propose EMIP (Embodied Multi-Party Interaction Platform), a virtual environment platform built on Minecraft. Through an Internet-based client-server architecture, EMIP connects multiple humans and multiple AI agents to the same virtual environment and supports full-duplex speech communication and simultaneous physical interaction. It provides interfaces based on the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for environmental observation, physical action execution, and audio input and output, enabling researchers to develop their own agent control methods using large language models (LLMs). Additional features include centralized control of an agent group through a single EMIP agent client, collaborative object transportation by multiple agents, and experimental support functions such as recording and retrieving observation histories. By integrating these features into a reusable platform, EMIP aims to support research on human-human, human-agent, and agent-agent cooperation under different participant configurations and agent control methods. Usage examples illustrate concurrent speech and physical action, task coordination, and overlapping speech. The source code for the platform is publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/AI-Humans-Lab/EMIP-Embodied-Multi-Party-Interaction-Platform).

FP-Prune: Rethinking Visual Token Pruning from an Information Gain Perspective. Visual token pruning can reduce the inference cost of vision language models, but its effectiveness depends on preserving complementary visual information under a limited token budget. A central challenge is to quantify the additional information a candidate token contributes beyond the retained set, a contribution that conventional scores based on attention or similarity struggle to capture directly. In this work, we revisit visual token pruning from the perspective of information gain and use mutual information to characterize the incremental value of candidate tokens. We further establish theoretically that frame potential serves as an effective surrogate for mutual information. Building on this observation, we propose FP-Prune, a training-free visual token pruning method that iteratively removes tokens with low information gain to preserve as much complementary visual information as possible. Experiments on three widely used VLMs and eight datasets demonstrate that FP-Prune outperforms baseline methods in both accuracy and inference efficiency. Further analysis shows that the surrogate objective closely aligns with model performance. Our work provides theoretical grounding and an effective method for visual token pruning.

From Vanishing Gradients to Recursive Self-Improvement: Evaluating the Most Influential Papers in Large Language Model Evolution (1997-2026). The rapid proliferation of Large Language Model (LLM) research makes it increasingly difficult to distinguish incremental refinements from true paradigm shifts. This review evaluates 22 of the most influential publications spanning nearly three decades (1997-2026), organized through a causal, chronologically anchored taxonomy centered on the author's birth year (1999). Beginning "before 1999" with how recurrent neural networks (RNNs) forgot earlier context (much like forgetting Chapter 1 by the time a reader reaches Chapter 9), we trace how Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks introduced a "bouncer" mechanism of forget, input, and output gates to selectively preserve long-term memory. We then examine how Word2Vec turned language into vector mathematics (king - male + female ~ queen), why sequential RNNs hit a parallelization wall, and how the Transformer's all-to-all attention weights launched the modern LLM era alongside a quadratic bottleneck. Next, we analyze why scaling parameters alone leaves capacity under-trained unless data scales equally (Chinchilla), how Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) left alignment superficial, and how that gap compounded into adversarial jailbreaks and single-direction refusal subspaces (J-space), where instructing a model not to think of a restricted concept surfaces it much like the human "red ball" paradox. Finally, we synthesize the current state of AI (2024-2026), encompassing recursive model collapse, autonomous reasoning-model jailbreak agents, machine-speed agentic intrusions, and closed-loop recursive self-improvement (AIDE^2).

Which Failure Does an Intervention Repair? When Agent Interventions Help, and Where Self-Evolving Skills Stall. An intervention that improves one agent can break another, and adding a stronger harness on top need not repair the damage. Agent interventions such as skills, harnesses, and extra inference budget are nonetheless usually credited with one average gain, measured under one setup. We ask instead when each intervention helps and which failure it repairs. A matched factorial study over nine benchmarks, four models, four skill conditions, four harness levels, and three budgets, with nearly 0.9 million trajectories, changes one axis at a time. No configuration is best everywhere, interventions interact rather than add, and a harness can absorb a skill's gain, rescue a failure the skill causes, or leave the gain intact. The failure left by the current system points to the fix: missing knowledge to a stronger model, execution errors to a richer harness. Yet feedback is not recovery: a matched recovery repairs mainly failures that leave a visible error signal. Skills that evolve from the agent's own experience hit a bottleneck: they rarely beat a short human-written skill, can learn dataset shortcuts, break when moved to another model, and cannot supply missing facts, which outside information does. A benchmark-level switch to the model favored by a 20-task labeled pilot achieves both higher performance and lower cost than always using the stronger model. Agent interventions should be judged by which failure they repair and under which configuration.

MetaSkill: Reusable Problem-Solving Methods for Adaptive Skill Orchestration in LLM Agents. Reusable skills provide specialized procedures, but large language model (LLM) agents must still determine how to organize and adapt their use. We introduce MetaSkill, a two-layer framework for reusing problem-solving methods across tasks and domains. The method layer selects from 26 curated methods and binds abstract roles to task objects. The execution layer uses the instantiated method to identify intermediate objectives, coordinate native skills, and guide repair or method reselection. On 89 SkillsBench tasks and 995 ToolHop examples, MetaSkill outperforms the evaluated baselines in all six configurations, with accuracy gains of 3.51-13.48% over the strongest baseline. Ablations support explicit method-guided orchestration beyond direct method injection and further gains from method reselection.

Neural Agent Compiler: Learning to Schedule Soft Dependencies. Large language model agents accomplish complex tasks by coordinating multiple reasoning steps and tool operations, which form dependencies among their operations. Existing orchestration methods primarily consider hard dependencies that determine when an operation can legally begin, but overlook soft dependencies, i.e., information that is not required for execution but may improve an already executable operation. We identify soft-dependency scheduling as an important problem in agent execution. To this end, we introduce Neural Agent Compiler (NAC), a learned scheduler that predicts the task-quality and resource consequences of three execution modes and selects the highest-utility legal mode at a scheduling boundary. NAC represents the executable continuation, pending information event, and resource state in a shared memory, and uses a utility function to adapt the consequence predictions to different resource preferences. Across AppWorld, WebShop, and $τ^2$-bench, NAC achieves 276/417 AppWorld task completions, a 74.69 WebShop Task Score, and 59/100 $τ^2$-bench successes. Additional studies show that the learned scheduler reduces execution work, establishing soft-dependency scheduling as a promising solution for orchestrating tool-using agents.

NoeVera: Can Knowledge Guide Experiments and Experiments Refine Knowledge?. With the growing demand for large language model (LLM) services, optimizing LLM serving systems is becoming increasingly complex, and the bottleneck is no longer predicting how a given configuration will perform. The harder problem is deciding what to investigate: which mechanisms matter for a workload, which configurations are worth testing, and what evidence a decision still needs. In this work, we present NoeVera, an agentic Second Brain that goes beyond just one-shot retrieval by turning papers, code, benchmarks, and experimental results into a persistent, provenance-preserving knowledge base with three planes: source evidence, reusable synthesis, and agent memory. Decision-aware retrieval assembles compact evidence packs, role-specific agents reason over them and invoke a simulator (Vidur or GAUSS) whenever quantitative support is needed, and every finding is written back as a scoped evidence record, so knowledge guides experiments and experiments refine knowledge. In configuration search over four serving scenarios, NoeVera comes within 5% of the optimum in a median of 6-7 simulator calls, versus 9 for Bayesian optimization and 15 for a knowledge-free agent with the same tools; on A100 GPUs, its representative configurations deliver ~1.30x vLLM-default throughput and meet every scenario's latency objective. When reused, provenance-preserving evidence records over-generalize on only 8% of applicability traps, versus 28% for a general-purpose agent memory. On the held-out 48-task split of a 72-task benchmark, NoeVera scores 29% higher than an equally equipped agent and 36% higher than its single-call retrieval counterpart (0.80 vs. 0.62 and 0.59), and even when baselines receive NoeVera's own prompts, a statistically significant part of its evidence-evolution advantage remains.

Seeing Is Not Acting: WARD Diagnoses the Evidence-to-State-to-Action Gap in Longitudinal Clinical Agents. Large language models for longitudinal clinical care must revise their assessments and actions as patient information accumulates. However, benchmarks centered on isolated responses or final task outcomes provide limited insight into intermediate failures in evidence use, state updating, and action selection. We introduce WARD, a benchmark for evaluating how clinical agents translate accumulating evidence into patient-state judgments and timely, safe actions. WARD comprises 4,560 clinical tasks across seven clinical output domains, organized into 240 checkpoints from 40 longitudinal clinical trajectories spanning 95 hospitalizations. Its Longitudinal Track evaluates these tasks under controlled cumulative evidence. Its Interactive Track evaluates end-to-end, tool-mediated clinical management across 271 verifiable evidence items and 141 reference transitions. Across 12 models with scorable checkpoint outputs, evidence recognition consistently outpaces downstream state and action decisions, with linked-evidence nonresponse reaching 74.47--90.90\%. Models also struggle to retain and update information over time, while in the Interactive Track only 11.46\% of executed actions advance a reference transition. These results reveal a persistent evidence-to-state-to-action gap and highlight the need for process-level evaluation of longitudinal clinical agents.Code and data: https://github.com/Dingsuper-creator/WARD.

GameAnything: From Any Inspirations to Playable Game Worlds. AI-driven game development holds the potential to transform diverse human inspirations into interactive experiences. However, existing systems and benchmarks primarily focus on explicit development specifications, with limited support for adapting multimodal references and evaluating actual gameplay experiences. We introduce GameAnything, an open-source agentic platform that transforms multimodal inspirations into playable extensions of existing games through iterative development. GameAnything integrates coding agents with an independent playtesting critic, persistent development state, and reusable experience memory to support continuous refinement. We further present GameAnything-Bench, a benchmark spanning diverse reference modalities, game creation objectives, and gaming environments, with exploratory gameplay testing to assess both functional correctness and gameplay quality. Evaluations of nine coding agent configurations reveal that current agents can adapt reference content but still struggle with playable interactions and precise modifications. Moreover, multimodal references improve content fidelity, while iterative refinement yields substantial but varying improvements across agents. These findings highlight both the potential and remaining challenges of inspiration-driven game development.

Direct Feedback Policy Optimization for AI Coding Agents. AI coding agents generate, modify, and validate code through multi-turn interactions. Existing reinforcement learning methods often rely on sparse terminal rewards, making it difficult to assess how intermediate decisions affect task outcomes, and group-relative methods also require repeated sampling for each task. We propose Direct Feedback Policy Optimization (DFPO), a single-trajectory reinforcement learning algorithm that trains directly from a single trajectory. DFPO achieves higher task resolution rates than GSPO under matched base models and execution harnesses.

Fixed or Deleted? External Feedback Lets Cheaper AI Coding Agents Repair Rule Violations. Many defects violate project rules that the code itself does not reveal, such as layering constraints or required tests. We study whether LLM coding agents repair such violations better when an external checker reports them, with their location and a repair goal. Three models, a small, medium and large model, driven by an AI agent, worked on 25 pull requests with 31 planted defects in ten open-source projects, plus 5 correct controls, five times alone and five times with findings from CodeAssure (CA), a commercial checker. We also compare with GitHub Copilot code review, and compare CodeAssure's detection with nine free static-analysis tools run out of the box, including Semgrep and SonarQube Community. Counting a run as repaired only when the repaired code also compiles and keeps its feature, CA findings raised the repair rate from 26% to 69% for the smallest model, from 46% to 90% for the medium model and from 45% to 93% for the largest model (pull-request-level p < 0.001), and from 39% to 84% over all runs. Every Java, TypeScript and Python repair compiled. We found that agents often cleared a defect by deleting a newly added file. Metrics based on whether the defect is gone count feature deletion as a success. The largest model alone did so in 44 of 125 runs. CA includes a check for deleted files that largely prevents this. In an ablation with the check turned off, removals rose from 9 to 65 out of 375 runs and the repair rate fell to 54% (small), 70% (medium) and 85% (large model). The CA workflow also outperformed Copilot code review (p < 0.001). Together, the free tools detected 8 of the 31 defects, and CA detected all 31. With CA, the medium model repaired 90% of runs, against 45% for the largest model alone, at about one fifth of the mean cost per run ($0.17 against $0.91).

ContextFact: Remembering Facts in Context for Long-Term Conversational Agents. Agents built on large language models must maintain continuity across repeated interactions with users. However, long-term conversations scatter facts across turns and sessions, making it difficult to retrieve the right evidence with enough context. Memory for such conversations must therefore preserve facts with their context while keeping evidence selectively accessible. We first study how memory construction and retrieval-unit boundaries affect answerability and evidence access. Reading the entire memory bank reveals gaps that cannot be resolved by retrieval selection alone, showing that some context must be preserved during memory construction. Adjacent-turn grouping improves evidence access at matched unique-turn budgets, while wider windows do not consistently help. This motivates keeping fact-specific context local while organizing cross-session evidence separately. We propose ContextFact, which links context-preserving fact memories with source-grounded entity representations. Within sessions, it gathers the context needed to interpret each fact. Across sessions, it aligns recurring referents and revisits the source dialogue to reconstruct coherent entity representations linked to the supporting facts. At query time, ContextFact retrieves fact and entity views, reranks them independently, and uses entity-linked expansion to surface related facts; complete entity representations then provide organized cross-session evidence. With Qwen3.5-27B as the backbone, ContextFact achieves state-of-the-art performance while using only $21\%$ of the evidence tokens consumed by the strongest evaluated baseline, obtaining $86.49\%$ overall judge accuracy on LoCoMo and $91.00\%$ on LongMemEval-S. Controlled ablations support context-preserving fact boundaries and source-grounded entity reconstruction, while entity readout improves multi-hop accuracy beyond adding more facts.

Can an Agent Trust Its Own Zoom? Cross-Magnification Provenance Verification for Whole-Slide Images. Visual agents navigate whole-slide images through magnified observations associated with claimed locations. However, a visually plausible observation does not necessarily originate from its claimed location, particularly across magnifications and in regions with similar tissue structures. We formulate cross-magnification provenance verification (CMPV) to evaluate whether visual evidence supports a claimed spatial association, recover the source when possible, and abstain when evidence is insufficient. We introduce PyraFault, a benchmark of 3.06 million coordinate-supervised examples from 2,200 cases across five TCGA cohorts, covering within-context substitutions, absent-source faults, and geometric perturbations. We further propose ZoomTrace, a claim-independent verifier that estimates the observation's source before evaluating its agreement with the claimed location. It combines physical-scale alignment, visual retrieval, geometric refinement, and reliability estimation using spatially disjoint competing matches. On 503,320 test examples, ZoomTrace achieves 0.969 AUPRC and 0.987 AUROC, compared with 0.789 and 0.903 for Efficient LoFTR. Further evaluations reveal trade-offs in reliability estimation and limitations in vision-language models, cross-dataset retrieval, and calibration. Integrating ZoomTrace into visual agent tool paths reduces exposure to corrupted observations and silent failures, while downstream accuracy improvements depend on the agent and verification threshold.

The Retry Tax: Why Static Same-Task Retries Can Cost More per Completion. Retrying an agent after failure can complete more tasks while increasing the cost per completion. We study a static policy that stops at verified success or an attempt cap and otherwise resets the original prompt and workspace without passing feedback to the next request. Under stationary task success probabilities, independent attempts conditional on the task, and a common attempt cost, easier tasks tend to succeed earlier. When task success probabilities differ, the unresolved mix shifts toward harder tasks. Specializing classical survivor selection, we show that cost per completion is at least as high as in one-shot serving and that marginal cost per additional completion is nondecreasing wherever the completion increments are positive. These are different quantities: one averages spending over all completions, while the other prices the completions added by another attempt. We then arrange each task's existing benchmark runs in different orders, stop each sequence at verified success or the attempt cap, and average the resulting completion and spending at each supported cap. For one OpenHands configuration, replay estimates completion of 59.7 percent with one attempt and 70.0 percent with four, while cost per completion rises from about USD 0.70 to USD 1.32. The recorded trade-off describes fixed configurations on the available tasks. Choosing a cap requires comparing the additional spending with the application's value for the additional completions.

DeepDOSReasoner: Physics-Grounded Reasoning for Density-of-States Prediction and Materials Discovery. Predicting a material's behavior from its atomic structure is a longstanding goal of the physical sciences. The electronic and phonon densities of states (eDOS and phDOS) govern key electronic, optical, vibrational, and thermodynamic properties, yet their calculation using density functional theory (DFT) is costly: about 60% of Materials Project entries lack eDOS and over 80% lack phDOS. Existing crystal-to-spectrum models rely on pooled structural representations and pointwise regression, which blur spectral features and violate total-state conservation. Here we introduce DeepDOSReasoner, a physics-grounded framework that decodes spectra through atom-to-energy source attention and refines the normalized DOS through learned continuity-equation transport, enforcing nonnegativity and total-state conservation by construction. DeepDOSReasoner achieves the highest prediction accuracy across all evaluated metrics for both eDOS and phDOS, recovers element-resolved contributions without supervision, and most reliably identifies rare valence-band (VB) gaps. In a prospective screen of 8,106 uncharted materials validated by new DFT calculations, its predictions remain the most accurate among the methods evaluated, with 25 of its top 50 candidates confirmed as VB-gap materials. Three case studies spanning substituted compounds, photovoltaic chalcogenides, and a high-entropy alloy demonstrate transfer across materials classes. Ablations confirm that both stages are necessary, while the model retains comparable accuracy when trained on only 25% of the data. Predicting spectra in milliseconds enables exhaustive screening; we release predictions filling the missing eDOS for 91,405 and phDOS for 127,768 Materials Project entries. DeepDOSReasoner provides a blueprint for integrating machine learning with physical reasoning toward high-throughput spectral screening and autonomous materials discovery.

c3.name: forecasts / forecasting / chlorophyll / ocean
texts: Interactive deep-learning based interface for brain tumour segmentation. Brain tumour segmentation from MR images is an integral part of their treatment, either through surgical resection or radiotherapy. Both applications require a high degree of precision that can be difficult to ensure for all patients due to the high degree of variability in the size, shape, number, and location of these tumours. This leads to difficulties with their automatic segmentation via deep learning, which can display catastrophic segmentation errors when presented with images that differ, even subtly, in terms of the specific MR sequence used, which varies from vendor to vendor. This article presents a deep-learning-based interactive segmentation system that, while being fully automatic by default, has the capability of being easily corrected by human users, allowing them ensure sufficiently high brain tumour segmentation accuracy for all patients. This interface is evaluated both in terms of the accuracy of its automatic approach as well as its usability through a preliminary observational expert user study.

Tracing Uncertainties of Extreme El Niño Prediction to Mesoscale Ocean Currents. The predictability of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) has historically been linked to large-scale errors in models' initial conditions such as heat content and surface wind stress. Here we demonstrate that these slowly evolving errors may ultimately originate from mesoscale errors in initial oceanic states that are common in current models and ocean observation systems. This hidden source of ENSO forecast uncertainty, in terms of mesoscale ocean-current errors, is convincingly exposed by the conditional nonlinear optimal perturbation (CNOP) method applied to a differentiable ocean AI model. The CNOP-identified most influential current errors are strongly event-dependent. For the 1997/98 El Niño, the initial current errors in the eastern Pacific results in the largest forecast error through locally suppressing original subsurface warming. For the 2015/16 event, the dominate error originates from the western Pacific, which reorganizes upper ocean temperature structure and affects the eastern Pacific through the equatorial waveguide. Further analysis reveals that these current errors perturb mesoscale eddy count and eddy kinetic energy triggering large-scale temperature errors that hinder El Niño development. The timing of the maximum growth rate of the obtained CNOP error is well aligned with the spring predictability barrier of ENSO, and the error structures are reflected in simulated analysis errors caused by unresolved mesoscale currents. These findings extend the potential source of ENSO predictability beyond large-scale thermal signals, reveal for the first time an uncharted route of ENSO forecast failure, and provide an important physical basis for targeted ocean observations and data assimilation in the future.

Logically Consistent Accurate Forecasts. Agentic forecasting systems based on large language models (LLMs) are now competitive with expert human forecasters, but these systems still suffer from a critical limitation: the inability to produce forecasts that are logically consistent. For example, forecasts for related events often fail to satisfy the axioms of probability, which in turn implies that related forecasts cannot simultaneously be correct and undermines their utility for decision makers. Enforcing consistency is not trivial -- naive approaches (e.g., projection onto the set of consistent forecasts) can degrade accuracy. We argue that the key to overcoming the apparent tradeoff between consistency and accuracy lies in the reasoning which supports each forecast. We finetune a supervisory language model that leverages this reasoning to jointly reconcile inconsistencies while improving the accuracy of related forecasts. On ForecastBench, our method improves the Brier score of a retrieval-augmented GPT-5.1 forecaster by 9.3% while reducing measures of structural inconsistency by 82-90%. We interrogate our method via a comprehensive series of baselines and ablations, and find that no alternative method matches our gains in consistency and accuracy simultaneously.

An AI-enabled high-resolution chlorophyll-a forecasting model that outperforms the operational global biogeochemical system. Surface chlorophyll-a concentration is a key indicator of marine phytoplankton variability, and short-term forecasts of its distribution provide advance information for marine ecosystem monitoring and management. However, interactions between physical transport and biological processes complicate chlorophyll-a forecasting, and simulating these coupled processes with conventional numerical models imposes substantial computational demands. Here we introduce ChlCast, an AI model that generates daily forecasts of surface chlorophyll-a concentration over a 10-day horizon at approximately 4-km resolution between 60$^\circ$S and 60$^\circ$N. ChlCast combines factorized spatiotemporal convolutions with a multiscale architecture to learn from historical chlorophyll-a fields and climatological information. Compared with the operational 0.25$^\circ$ Copernicus global ocean biogeochemical forecasting system, ChlCast reduces mean absolute error and root mean square error by 70.74% and 47.63%, respectively, against satellite-derived Level-4 chlorophyll-a fields, and by 35.03% and 13.07% against independent BGC-Argo in situ observations. Coastal case studies further show that the 4-km forecasts retain coastal gradients and localized concentration maxima that are weakened by coarse-grid averaging. These results demonstrate the potential of observation-driven deep learning for high-resolution forecasting of surface chlorophyll-a variability at the near-global scale.

AeroJEPA: A Two-Stage Framework for Aerosol Forecasting with Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning. Aerosol forecasting requires integrating sparse ground observations and modeling meteorologically driven concentration evolution and spatial structure. However, analysis-initialized forecasts make limited explicit use of historical observations, while pointwise regression tends to smooth local variations and provides limited constraints on fine spatial structures. In this work, we propose AeroJEPA, a two-stage joint-embedding predictive framework for regional surface PM$_{2.5}$ forecasting. Specifically, Stage I fuses historical observations, model backgrounds, and meteorological information to predict an initial future state, meteorological conditions, and multi-scale structures. Morphology-guided encoding and joint-embedding predictive supervision support learning future spatial representations, supplementing concentration regression with structural constraints. Stage II uses predicted meteorology to guide state refinement and incorporates coarse- and fine-scale structures into state updates and decoding to generate the concentration field at a single future time step. Experiments show that AeroJEPA reduces gridded and independent-station RMSE by 17.23\% and 7.90\%, respectively, relative to PFGNet, while improving spatial consistency with analysis fields. In a 48 h recursive forecasting case study, AeroJEPA generally achieves lower RMSE and MAE than the numerical forecasts across the forecast period, indicating promising short- to medium-range forecasting performance.

texts: TotalSegmentator Aorta Report: Automated Aortic Diameter Measurement at 11 Standardized Landmarks on CT Images. Purpose: To develop and evaluate a fully automated, open-source tool that measures aortic diameters at 11 standardized landmarks from the aortic annulus to the bifurcation on any CT image, following current guideline recommendations. Materials and Methods: This retrospective single-center study included 239 arterial phase CT angiography examinations of 230 patients (median age, 65 years [range, 18-99 years]; 163 men) performed between April 2025 and October 2026 (209 electrocardiographically [ECG] gated). The tool locates landmarks from TotalSegmentator segmentations of aortic branches and vertebrae and measures the maximum diameter at each. A senior radiologist reviewed and, where needed, corrected the automated measurements to create the reference standard. Agreement was assessed with mean absolute error (MAE), bias, and differences greater than 2 mm. Results: Across all landmarks, MAE was 1.06 mm (95% CI: 0.91, 1.22), and 86.6% (95% CI: 84.4, 88.5) of differences were 2 mm or less. The tool measured slightly larger diameters (bias, 0.45 mm [95% CI: 0.34, 0.57]). The sinuses of Valsalva had the largest MAE (2.17 mm [95% CI: 1.59, 2.86]). For 1.2% of landmarks, the automatic measurement failed. Examination-level MAE did not differ significantly by pathology, atherosclerosis grade (P=.95), or ECG gating (P=.14). Examinations with mural thrombus more often had an MAE greater than 2 mm (50% [95% CI: 31, 69] vs 20%; P=.03). Conclusion: The tool measured aortic diameters at 11 landmarks along the entire aorta with an MAE of about 1 mm, below published interreader variability. Agreement was lower at the aortic root and with mural thrombus. Code availability: The tool is open source and freely available at https://github.com/wasserth/TotalSegmentator.

Is Abliteration Getting Harder? Not Uniformly: Refusal Removal by Direction-Based Ablation and ARA in Heretic on the Qwen3.8, Gemma 4, Olmo 3.1 and Mistral Small 3.2 LLMs Versus Their Predecessors. Abliteration, a fine-tuning-free weight edit, removes refusal from open-weight large language models (LLMs). The developer of Arbitrary-Rank Ablation (ARA), an optimisation-based variant, reports that direction-based abliteration, which ablates a refusal direction, increasingly fails on newer models. On five release pairs, refusal removal did not become uniformly harder. Qwen2.5-32B and Qwen3.8-27B, Gemma-2-27B and Gemma-4-31B, OLMo-2-32B and Olmo-3.1-32B, Mistral-Small-2409 and Mistral-Small-3.2, and Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen3.5-4B were edited in Heretic 2.0 by three or four direction-based methods (difference-in-means, MPOA, SOM and, on the small pair, J-space) and ARA under the same prompts, nominal search budget, first-token KL divergence cap and selection rule; removal counted as harder when the automatic WildGuard judge found more of 972 held-out harmful prompts (JailbreakBench, XSTest, StrongREJECT, HarmBench and an author-compiled malicious-code bank) still refused. After direction-based removal, newer releases retained -1 to +37 percentage points more refusal, and after ARA -26 to +34. With run-to-run variance included, between-pair heterogeneity of the direction-based effect ranged from high to low with the scale and variance model (I^2 20-80%). ARA lost less effectiveness than direction-based methods in Gemma and OLMo and more in Qwen; each verdict rests on one ARA run, and some changed with the divergence budget or variance model. In Gemma the direction-based increase came from the malicious-code bank and reversed on public sets. Contrary to prediction, keyword counts at the tool's window did not undercount judged refusal on average, but differed by a mean 7 points per model. Audits of a single pair, method or prompt source can reach opposite conclusions. Whether a newer model resisted removal depended on the release pair, method and budget, not on generation alone.

Can Large Language Models Optimize Pretrained Neural Network Weights? A Multi-Phase Empirical Evaluation of Gradient-Free Editing in YOLO26 Object Detection. Direct weight editing offers a gradient-free alternative to fine-tuning pretrained detectors, but its generalization and the value of large language model (LLM) guidance remain uncertain. We evaluate five experimental phases using YOLO26 models and MS COCO, comparing deterministic scaling, random perturbations, differential evolution, CMA-ES, structured interventions, real local-LLM proposals, failure-aware guidance, and hybrid LLM-CMA-ES against a matched random-policy control. Optimization uses native Ultralytics mAP50-95 on 1,000 COCO Val2017 images; selected candidates are assessed on a disjoint, previously examined 1,500-image subset, with COCO API AP50-95 reported separately where available. Increasing the CMA-ES budget from 8 to 250 evaluations raised development gains from +0.11 to +0.28 percentage points, while selection changes remained negative (-0.03 to -0.12 points); the 250-evaluation result uses one seed. The hybrid LLM approach showed no statistically established advantage over random-policy guidance (p = 0.612, 0.369, and 0.694 at budgets 8, 25, and 50). Five-seed YOLO26m replication yielded a COCO API AP difference of +0.004 points (95% CI: -0.026 to +0.034). Of 225 archived LLM proposals, 53 satisfy the final strict schema; early tensor-level execution cannot be fully verified. Genuine LLM-mediated weight editing is feasible, but the tested approaches did not demonstrate consistent transfer beyond the development subset or a measurable LLM advantage.

GEM-MM: Reducing VLM Hallucination with Entropy-Guided Preference Alignment. Vision-language models (VLMs) are routinely aligned with offline pairwise RLHF objectives, but multimodal preference data is scarce and treats every response token as equally informative. Under a small preference budget, pair construction becomes nearly irrelevant: standard DPO-style, image-conditional, and self-improvement objectives all perform within 1.1 points on MM-RLHF metrics and 0.5 points on hallucination rates, matching the SFT baseline. We call this entropy-blind preference optimization: the learning signal ignores policy uncertainty, which in chain-of-thought VLMs concentrates on specific fork tokens where visual claims are made. We introduce GEM-MM, extending entropy-guided preference modeling to VLMs. It samples on-policy candidates, rewards high-entropy reasoning forks, penalizes uncertain final answers, and updates the model via group-normalized policy gradients. On a 3000-prompt MM-RLHF budget with Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, GEM-MM achieves the best entropy-depth preference score (61.7% vs. 57.3-58.4% baselines) and implicit-reward accuracy (41.4%). Crucially, it reduces AMBER hallucination from 23.4-24.0 to 20.6 and CHAIR from 5.0-5.1 to 4.6 at matched caption coverage. It also ranks best on all three HallusionBench granularities, with a conservative operating point raising the near-chosen rate to 62.4%. An off-the-shelf multimodal reward model ranks GEM-MM first, and two such models independently confirm our main ablations (p < 0.001). We report confidence intervals, paired significance tests, metric-reward functional overlaps, and document a collapse mode when exceeding the fair budget.
